notes.summary: Computer security covers harmful software (malware), common attacks, and the tools that protect us. Tier 2 asks 2–3 direct questions, mostly "which malware/attack is this?" and "what does a firewall/encryption do?".

concepts.title: Malware
concepts.body:
• Virus: attaches to a host file and spreads when that file runs.
  • Worm: copies itself across networks on its own, without a host file.
  • Trojan horse: looks like useful software but does harm in the background.
  • Ransomware: encrypts your files and demands payment (e.g. WannaCry, 2017).
  • Spyware / Keylogger: secretly records activity or keystrokes. Adware: shows unwanted ads.
  • The first PC virus is usually cited as Brain (1986, from Pakistan); Creeper was the first self-replicating program.

concepts.title: Attacks
concepts.body:
• Phishing: fake email/website to steal passwords or card details. Vishing = by voice call; Smishing = by SMS.
  • DoS / DDoS: flooding a server so real users cannot use it (DDoS uses many computers, often a botnet).
  • Spoofing: faking an identity (email, IP). Man-in-the-middle: secretly intercepting communication.
  • Hacking: unauthorised access. Ethical (white-hat) hackers test systems with permission.

concepts.title: Protection
concepts.body:
• Firewall: hardware or software that filters network traffic by rules.
  • Antivirus: detects and removes malware.
  • Encryption: turns plaintext into unreadable ciphertext; decryption reverses it. Symmetric = one shared key; asymmetric = public key + private key.
  • Digital signature: made with the sender's private key, checked with the sender's public key.
  • Two-factor authentication (2FA): password + OTP / fingerprint. CAPTCHA tells humans from bots.

varieties.name: Identify the malware
varieties.how: Look for the key behaviour: needs a host (virus), spreads alone (worm), disguised (trojan), asks for money (ransomware).

example.q: A program secretly records every key a user presses. What is it?
steps: It records keystrokes, so it is spyware.

varieties.name: Identify the attack
varieties.how: Match the method: fake message (phishing), flooding (DoS), fake identity (spoofing).

example.q: You get an SMS saying "Your bank KYC expires today, click this link". What attack is this?
steps: Because it comes by SMS, it is called smishing.

varieties.name: Security tools
varieties.how: Know what each tool does and which key is used where in encryption and signatures.

example.q: To send a secret message to Ravi using public-key encryption, which key do you use?
steps: Anyone may encrypt with Ravi's public key.
Only Ravi's private key can decrypt it.

tips: Worm = "walks" on its own; virus needs a host file.
WannaCry (2017) is the standard ransomware example.
Encrypt with the receiver's public key; sign with your own private key.
traps: A firewall is not an antivirus: it filters traffic, it does not clean infected files.
A Trojan does not replicate itself, unlike a virus or worm.
Phishing is an attack (social engineering), not a type of malware.

questions.q: Malware that copies itself and spreads across a network on its own, without attaching to a host file, is a:
questions.solution: A worm is self-replicating and travels across networks by itself. A virus needs a host file to spread.

questions.q: The main job of a firewall is to:
options: Filter incoming and outgoing network traffic
questions.solution: A firewall checks network traffic against rules and blocks what is not allowed. Removing viruses is the job of antivirus software.

questions.q: Sending fake emails that look like they come from a bank, to steal passwords, is called:
questions.solution: Phishing uses fake messages or websites to trick people into revealing passwords or card details.

questions.q: A program that pretends to be a useful game but secretly harms the computer is a:
questions.solution: A Trojan horse hides harmful code inside software that looks useful, like the wooden horse of Troy.

questions.q: Converting readable data (plaintext) into an unreadable form (ciphertext) is called:
questions.solution: Encryption converts plaintext to ciphertext so only someone with the key can read it. Decryption is the reverse.

questions.q: An attack that floods a website with so much traffic that real users cannot reach it is a:
questions.solution: A DoS attack overloads a server. When many computers (a botnet) do it together, it is a DDoS attack.

questions.q: WannaCry (2017), which locked files on computers worldwide and demanded Bitcoin payment, is an example of:
questions.solution: WannaCry encrypted victims' files and demanded a ransom in Bitcoin, which is exactly what ransomware does.

questions.q: A digital signature is created using the:
questions.solution: The sender signs with their own private key. Anyone can then verify the signature with the sender's public key, which proves who sent it and that it was not changed.

flashcards.back: Virus needs a host file; worm spreads on its own over networks
Malware disguised as useful software; does not self-replicate
Fake email or website / voice call / SMS
Distributed Denial of Service: many machines flood a server
Signed with sender's private key, verified with sender's public key
